bodyText:
What is Software?

Software is the set of programs, procedures and data that instruct computer hardware to perform a task. Without software, hardware is only a collection of electronic components with no instructions to follow. Software is broadly classified into two categories: system software and application software.

System Software

System software is software that manages and controls computer hardware so that application software can run. It acts as an interface between the user, the application programs and the hardware. The most important example of system software is the operating system. Other examples include device drivers, language translators such as compilers and interpreters, and utility programs.

System software generally runs in the background, starts when the computer is switched on, and is essential for the computer to function at all. It is usually written in low-level languages and is supplied by the computer manufacturer or the operating system vendor.

Application Software

Application software is software designed to perform a specific task for the user, such as writing a document, editing a photograph, browsing the internet or playing a game. It runs on top of system software and cannot work without an operating system underneath it.

Application software is of two kinds. General-purpose application software, such as word processors, spreadsheets and web browsers, can be used by many different users for many different tasks. Specific-purpose or customised application software is written for one particular organisation or task, such as a payroll system, a hospital management system or a railway reservation system.

Key Differences

The fundamental difference is one of purpose and dependence. System software manages the computer itself, while application software serves the user. Application software depends on system software, but system software does not depend on any particular application. System software is general and hardware-oriented, whereas application software is task-oriented and user-oriented.
keyPoints: Software is the set of programs and data that instruct computer hardware to perform a task.
System software manages and controls computer hardware so that application software can run.
The operating system is the most important example of system software.
Device drivers, compilers, interpreters and assemblers are examples of system software.
Application software performs a specific task for the user, such as word processing or web browsing.
Application software runs on top of system software and cannot work without an operating system.
Microsoft Word, Microsoft Excel and web browsers are examples of general-purpose application software.
A payroll system or a hospital management system is an example of specific-purpose application software.
System software is hardware-oriented and user-independent, while application software is user-oriented and task-specific.
System software generally starts automatically when the computer is switched on, whereas application software is started by the user when needed.

bodyText:
What is an Operating System?

An operating system (OS) is system software that manages all the hardware and software resources of a computer and provides common services for programs. It controls the processor, memory, input and output devices and files, and it provides the interface through which the user interacts with the machine. Without an operating system, a user would have to control the hardware directly.

Batch Operating System

In a batch operating system, similar jobs are grouped together into batches and executed one after another without user interaction. The user submits a job, and the system processes the whole batch automatically. This was the earliest form of operating system and was used on large mainframe computers, but it gives no interaction while a job is running and the processor may sit idle between jobs.

Multiprogramming Operating System

A multiprogramming operating system keeps several programs in memory at the same time. When one program waits for an input or output operation, the processor switches to another program instead of sitting idle. This improves processor utilisation and overall throughput, although the user still does not interact with a running program directly.

Time-Sharing Operating System

A time-sharing operating system allows many users to use the computer at the same time by dividing processor time into small slices and switching rapidly between users. Each user feels as though they have the whole computer to themselves. Time-sharing is interactive, so users can enter commands and receive an immediate response.

Real-Time Operating System

A real-time operating system (RTOS) is designed to process data and respond within a strict, guaranteed time limit. It is used where a delayed response could cause failure, such as in aircraft control systems, medical equipment, industrial robots and air-traffic control. In a hard real-time system the deadline must always be met, while in a soft real-time system occasional small delays are acceptable.

Distributed and Other Types

A distributed operating system manages a group of independent computers connected by a network so that they work together as a single system, sharing resources such as files and printers. A single-user operating system allows only one user at a time, while a multi-user operating system allows several users to work on the same computer simultaneously. An embedded operating system is built into a device such as a washing machine, a microwave oven or a car engine controller.
keyPoints: An operating system manages all hardware and software resources of a computer and provides services for programs.
A batch operating system groups similar jobs into batches and executes them without user interaction.
Batch operating systems were the earliest form of operating system, used on mainframe computers.
A multiprogramming operating system keeps several programs in memory at the same time to improve processor utilisation.
A time-sharing operating system divides processor time into small slices so many users can work interactively at once.
A real-time operating system must respond within a strict, guaranteed time limit.
Hard real-time systems must always meet their deadlines, while soft real-time systems tolerate occasional small delays.
A distributed operating system makes a network of independent computers work together as a single system.
A single-user operating system serves one user at a time, while a multi-user operating system serves several users simultaneously.
MS-DOS is an example of a single-user operating system, while UNIX and Linux are examples of multi-user operating systems.

bodyText:
What are Utility Programs?

Utility programs, also called utilities or service programs, are system software tools that help to manage, maintain and protect a computer system. They do not create documents or perform a user's main task; instead they keep the system running efficiently, safely and smoothly. Most operating systems supply a set of built-in utilities, and additional utilities can be installed separately.

Common Utility Programs and Their Uses

  • Antivirus software: detects, blocks and removes viruses, worms, spyware and other malicious programs, and protects files and data from infection.
  • Disk defragmenter: rearranges fragmented files on a hard disk so that the parts of each file are stored together, which improves access speed.
  • Disk cleanup: removes temporary files, cached data and other unnecessary files to free up disk space.
  • Backup utility: copies important files and system data to another location so that they can be restored after data loss, hardware failure or accidental deletion.
  • File compression utility: reduces the size of files, for example into ZIP format, so that they take less storage space and are faster to send over a network.
  • Disk checker and repair tool: scans a disk for errors, bad sectors and file system problems and repairs them where possible.
  • File manager: allows the user to organise, copy, move, rename, search and delete files and folders.
  • Uninstaller: removes a program completely, including its files and settings, when it is no longer needed.

Why Utilities Matter

Regular use of utilities prevents common problems: antivirus software protects against data theft and corruption, backup protects against total data loss, disk cleanup and defragmentation keep the system fast, and compression saves storage and bandwidth. For examination purposes, remember that utilities are classified as system software, not application software, because they serve the computer system rather than a specific user task.

bodyText:
Open Source Software

Open source software is software whose source code is freely available for anyone to inspect, modify and distribute. Users are not only allowed to run the program, but also to study how it works and to adapt it to their needs, usually under a licence such as the GNU General Public License (GPL). Well-known examples include the Linux operating system, the LibreOffice office suite and the Firefox web browser.

The open source movement grew out of the free software movement founded by Richard Stallman, who established the Free Software Foundation in 1985. The Linux kernel itself was created by Linus Torvalds in 1991 and is developed collaboratively by programmers around the world.

Proprietary Software

Proprietary software, also called closed source software, is software whose source code is kept secret by its owner. Users buy a licence to use the program, but they may not inspect, modify or redistribute its code. Examples include Microsoft Windows, Microsoft Office and Adobe Photoshop. Proprietary software is usually sold for a fee and supported by the company that owns it, which also controls updates and new versions.

Choosing Between the Two

Open source software is usually free of licence cost and can be customised, but the user may need technical skill and community support rather than a company help desk. Proprietary software usually offers dedicated customer support, regular tested updates and professional documentation, but it costs money and locks the user into the vendor's decisions. Neither model is always better: the right choice depends on cost, support needs, customisation and security requirements.

The Linux kernel was created by Linus Torvalds in 1991.
Linux, LibreOffice and Firefox are examples of open source software.
The GNU General Public License (GPL) is a widely used open source licence.
Proprietary software, also called closed source software, keeps its source code secret.
Users of proprietary software buy a licence to use it but may not modify or redistribute its code.
Microsoft Windows, Microsoft Office and Adobe Photoshop are examples of proprietary software.
Open source software is usually free of licence cost and can be customised by its users.
Proprietary software usually provides dedicated customer support and regular updates from its owning company.
